title: Global Risk Governance Monitor: Global Catastrophic and Existential Risks

citation: Cherlet, J. (2026). GlobalRisks dataset v4.0, Global Risk Governance Monitor, globalriskgovernance.org
companion_dataset: RiskGovernance.json lists the multilateral governance mechanisms for each risk in this file.
changes: Version 4.0 (27 November 2026). All text was rewritten in short, full sentences. The assessments of likelihood and impact did not change.
A one-sentence summary was added for every risk.

Structure: the bands of the likelihood and impact scales are now objects with a label and a range or definition. Roots and channels have a code and a name. Sources are a list of report identifiers with an optional note. Failure modes are also given as a list. Multipliers list the risks they amplify as codes.

methodology.purpose: This dataset lists the global catastrophic and existential risks that humanity faces in the 21st century. The risks are organised as a risk tree. For each risk, the dataset gives a relative assessment of two things: how likely the risk is to reach global catastrophic scale by 2100, and how severe its impact would be. Both are given as ranges, not as single values. The dataset is the risk layer of the Global Risk Governance Monitor (globalriskgovernance.org).

terminology.framing: The phrase 'global catastrophic and existential risks' comes from the UN Pact for the Future (A/RES/79/1, 2024). The UN Global Risk Reports of 2024 and 2026 define a global risk as 'an event or condition that would have a significant negative impact on a large portion of humanity and the planet'.
terminology.global_catastrophic_risk: A global catastrophic risk is the risk of an event severe enough to significantly harm or set back human civilisation at the global scale. This follows the US Global Catastrophic Risk Management Act, as used by RAND and HSOAC (2024). A common working threshold is more than 10 million deaths or more than US$10 trillion in damage. Such an event is global in scope, but humanity can recover from it. The dataset also adopts the broader definition of Bostrom and Ćirković: a risk that might seriously damage human well-being on a global scale.
terminology.existential_risk: An existential risk is a global catastrophic risk of a special kind (Bostrom; Ord). It threatens the premature extinction of humanity, or the permanent and drastic destruction of its long-term potential. By definition, there is no recovery from it.
terminology.civilization_collapse: Civilisation collapse is the concept that links the two. It is a relatively rapid breakdown of social and political order, with large-scale death, economic decline and the disintegration of government. It can be the result of a global catastrophe. It is also a pathway by which a catastrophe becomes existential.

inclusion_criteria.rule: A hazard is listed as a risk only if it meets all four criteria.
inclusion_criteria.criterion_1_scope: Global scope. The consequences are global, or can plausibly cascade to global scale. They are not confined to one nation or region.
inclusion_criteria.criterion_2_severity: Catastrophic or terminal severity, by any one of three routes. Route (a) is mortality: about 10 million deaths or more. Route (b) is civilisational function: a comparable setback in governance, critical infrastructure or the functioning of the Earth system, or about US$10 trillion or more in damage. Route (c) is well-being: a widespread, severe and sustained loss of basic welfare (food, water, shelter, health, physical safety or fundamental freedoms) for about 10% of the world's population or more, which is about 800 million people, or the forced displacement of about 100 million people or more. Route (c) follows Bostrom and Ćirković ('serious damage to human well-being on a global scale'), the UN ('a large portion of humanity'), the World Economic Forum ('population'), RAND (societal instability and reduced human capabilities) and the Sendai Framework ('people affected'). The numbers are working thresholds and can be revised. Risks that can also cause extinction or a permanent loss of potential are flagged as existential.
inclusion_criteria.criterion_3_plausibility: Plausibility. The probability is not negligible within the period studied, from the recent past to 2100. Mechanisms that are astronomically improbable, such as a nearby gamma-ray burst or vacuum decay, are noted but not listed.
inclusion_criteria.criterion_4_distinctness: Distinctness. The hazard has a distinct role in the tree (root cause, terminal hazard, multiplier or cascade) and a distinct primary mechanism of harm. Candidates that share a mechanism are merged. A label that hides two mechanisms is split: natural and engineered pandemics are separate, and so are nuclear explosions and chemical toxicity. A candidate that is the worst case of another risk (tipping points) or its precursor (inequality before lock-in; conventional war between great powers before nuclear war) is folded into that risk. Whether a risk has its own governance regime plays no part in inclusion.
structural_principles: Keep the roles apart. Roots cause risks. Terminal hazards are the events that happen. Multipliers raise the likelihood or severity of those events. Cascades are how an event becomes global. Only terminal hazards are placed on the likelihood and impact scales, because only they materialise.

Treat general-purpose enabling technologies as multipliers, not as risks, with one exception. AI is part of the hazards that it facilitates, and it is named once as a multiplier. It is a terminal hazard only where the technology itself becomes the danger: the loss of human control over advanced AI.
Keep 'unknown unknowns' as an explicit risk, following Ord and Bostrom's 'Type-0' vulnerability.

risk_tree.basis: The tree is adapted from the work of Nick Bostrom. It uses the division by Bostrom and Ćirković (2008) into risks from nature, risks from unintended consequences and risks from hostile acts. It uses the recurring channels of human-made catastrophe from the Vulnerable World Hypothesis (2019). It also uses Bostrom's four failure modes: bangs, crunches, shrieks and whimpers.

A.name: Nature
A.description: Hazards that do not depend on human activity. They are astrophysical, geophysical, solar or biological (the natural emergence of a pathogen). Humans can only control their exposure and their preparedness.

B.name: Human activity and technology
B.description: Every other catastrophic risk originates in what humans do and, above all, in the technologies that humans have developed.

B1.name: Unintended, cumulative consequences
B1.description: Many actors each add a little, and together they destabilise the Earth system.

B2.name: Deliberate use of destructive capability
B2.description: Weapons are used on purpose and cause a catastrophe.

B3.name: Loss of control over powerful technology
B3.description: A technology runs away from its makers. This includes an unforeseen property of a new invention.

B4.name: Loss of collective control over the human future
B4.description: Concentrated power or fragile systems harden into a state from which there is no return.

crunch.label: Crunch
crunch.definition: Humanity survives, but its potential is permanently curtailed.

shriek.label: Shriek
shriek.definition: A flawed future is locked in.

node_types.terminal_hazards: There are 14 terminal hazards. These are the events that actually happen. They are the only nodes placed on the likelihood and impact scales.
node_types.multipliers: There are 3 multipliers. They are conditions that raise the probability or severity of the terminal hazards without being catastrophes in themselves. They are assessed in words and shown as a separate layer, never on the scales.
node_types.cascades: There are 5 cascades. They are the downstream channels through which almost any hazard becomes global: famine and agricultural failure, mass displacement, financial collapse, failure of critical infrastructure, and state failure. They are listed once and are never treated as risks.

risk_tree.tipping_points: Tipping points in the Earth system are not a risk of their own. They are the non-linear worst case of the two cumulative risks, climate change and biosphere collapse. They explain why the impact of those two risks ranges from Catastrophic to Near-existential.
tree: Root A, Nature: Asteroid / comet impact (N1); Supervolcanic eruption (N2); Severe space weather (N3); Natural pandemic (N4)
Root B, channel B1, Unintended, cumulative consequences: Climate change (E1); Biosphere collapse (E2)
Root B, channel B2, Deliberate use of destructive capability: Nuclear war (W1); Engineered pandemic (W2); Other WMD (W3)
Root B, channel B3, Loss of control over powerful technology: Uncontrolled advanced AI (T1); Failed geoengineering (T2); Unknown unknowns (T3)
Root B, channel B4, Loss of collective control over the human future: Permanent global power lock-in (F1); Civilisational systems collapse (F2)
Multipliers: Great-power rivalry (M1); Social fragmentation, disinformation, governance failure (M2); AI as amplifier (M3)
Cascades: famine; mass displacement; financial collapse; infrastructure failure; state failure

assessment_method.approach: The assessments are relative judgements on ordinal scales, made under deep uncertainty. They are aids for comparison, not forecasts. No point probabilities are given. Likelihood is kept separate from confidence, following the practice of the IPCC. Each terminal hazard is scored as a range. The modal value is its most probable catastrophic form. The tail is its worst case, which has a lower probability. Existential risk lies in the tail. For the two cumulative risks, the tail is a cascade of tipping points.

likelihood_scale.definition: The probability that the hazard reaches the global catastrophic threshold (criterion 2, by any route) at least once before 2100.

impact_scale.definition: Impact is assessed on five dimensions: mortality, decline in well-being, breadth, reversibility, and loss of potential for future generations. Reversibility counts as a step change: an outcome without recovery is categorically worse than any outcome with recovery.

I1.label: Severe
I1.definition: The global catastrophic threshold is reached through mortality (about 10 million deaths or more), loss of function (US$10 trillion or more) or loss of well-being (about 10% of humanity). Full recovery is possible.

I2.label: Catastrophic
I2.definition: About 100 million deaths or more, or a setback to the welfare of most of humanity. Recovery is possible but leaves lasting scars.

I3.label: Civilizational
I3.definition: About 1 billion deaths or more, or the collapse of global civilisation. Recovery is uncertain and would take generations.

I4.label: Near-existential
I4.definition: A collapse that threatens to become permanent. Humanity's potential is drastically and perhaps irreversibly curtailed.

I5.label: Existential
I5.definition: Extinction, or the permanent loss of humanity's potential, without recovery.

assessment_method.confidence: Confidence is stated for each hazard (High, Moderate, Low or Very low) and must be read together with the bands. Where sources diverge, the range is widened and the confidence is lowered. The estimates are not averaged.
assessment_method.evidence_base: The evidence consists of published structured estimates (Ord 2020), expert-judgement and forecasting exercises (Oxford FHI 2008, the Existential Risk Persuasion Tournament 2022, Metaculus, and the UN Global Risk Surveys of 2024 and 2026), the six reference reports, and historical base rates where they exist. Perception surveys are evidence about attention, not about the hazard. A shift in perception alone never moves a band.
assessment_method.dashboard_placement: On the interactive grid, the terminal hazards are placed on a grid with the likelihood bands as columns and the impact bands as rows, with at most one card per cell. Each hazard takes the cell of its modal values if that cell is free. Otherwise it takes the nearest free cell within its documented range, preferably by moving sideways. The row for Existential impact is not shown, because no hazard has extinction as its most likely outcome. The multipliers are shown in a separate row below the grid. Their position has no likelihood or impact meaning.
assessment_method.limitations: These are comparative judgements from a structured synthesis by a single analyst. They should be replaced by a formal structured expert elicitation. Likelihood and impact are never multiplied into one number. The hazards are scored as if they were independent, but they are correlated. The joint risk is therefore larger than the sum of the parts.

source_reports.title: United Nations, Global Risk Report 2024
source_reports.note: Covers 28 risks. Survey of 1,100 respondents in 136 countries. Includes a network of interconnections between risks and a set of 'global vulnerabilities'.

source_reports.title: United Nations, Global Risk Report 2026
source_reports.note: Covers the same 28 risks. Survey of 1,300 respondents, held from February to April 2026. Rates importance, imminence and preparedness, maps 705 links between risks, and works backwards from a large-scale war to its drivers.

source_reports.title: RAND / HSOAC, Global Catastrophic Risk Assessment (2024)
source_reports.note: Uses the definitions of the US Global Catastrophic Risk Management Act. Covers six hazards and several categories of consequence. Declines to assign probabilities.

source_reports.title: Global Challenges Foundation, Global Catastrophic Risks 2026
source_reports.note: Covers climate, ecological collapse, weapons of mass destruction, AI in military decision-making and asteroids. Frames them in terms of the stability of the Earth system.

source_reports.title: UK Government, National Risk Register 2025
source_reports.note: Scores national risks on likelihood and impact. Used here for the subset of risks with a global scope.

source_reports.title: World Economic Forum, Global Risks Report 2026
source_reports.note: Ranks more than 33 risks in five categories by perception.

source_reports.title: UN General Assembly, Pact for the Future (A/RES/79/1, 2024)
source_reports.note: Source of the phrase 'catastrophic and existential risks'.

source_reports.title: Bostrom (2002) Existential Risks; Bostrom (2019) The Vulnerable World Hypothesis; Bostrom & Ćirković (2008) Global Catastrophic Risks
source_reports.note: Source of the failure modes, the types of vulnerability, and the division into risks from nature, unintended consequences and hostile acts.

source_reports.title: Ord (2020) The Precipice
source_reports.note: Gives estimates of existential risk for this century and introduces the category of unknown risks.

source_reports.title: UN Independent International Scientific Panel on AI, first report (July 2026)
source_reports.note: Finds that there is 'no technical guarantee' that frontier AI systems follow instructions.

risks.name: Asteroid / comet impact

impact.dominant_dimensions: Mortality, breadth, and permanence in the worst case

risks.sources_note: The UN reports list this risk as 'Space-Based Event'.
risks.summary: A large asteroid or comet strikes Earth and darkens the sky for years.
risks.description: An object of 1 km or more would throw enough dust into the atmosphere to cause a global 'impact winter', with crop failure and mass mortality. An object of 10 km or more could plausibly cause human extinction. The probability is very low. Unlike most risks, it can be calculated from sky surveys. Toby Ord estimates the chance of an existential catastrophe from an impact at about 1 in 1,000,000 this century. In the UN Global Risk Report 2026, respondents expect a 'space-based event' to matter only after eight years or more. The event does not appear in the report's map of interconnected risks. The report names inadequate data and information as the main barrier to preparing for it.

risks.name: Supervolcanic eruption

impact.dominant_dimensions: Famine and loss of well-being, breadth

risks.sources_note: The UN reports cover it under 'Large-Scale Natural Hazard Risks', a category whose definition includes volcanic activity.
risks.summary: A super-eruption blocks sunlight for years and causes harvests to fail worldwide.
risks.description: An eruption of magnitude 8 on the Volcanic Explosivity Index would eject thousands of cubic kilometres of material. It would cause a 'volcanic winter' lasting several years, the collapse of harvests and possibly a famine that threatens civilisation. It is more probable than a large impact. Toby Ord estimates the existential risk at about 1 in 10,000 this century. It cannot currently be prevented.

risks.name: Severe space weather
risks.sources_note: The UN reports list this risk as 'Space-Based Event'.
risks.summary: An extreme solar storm knocks out power grids, satellites and communications across continents.
risks.description: A coronal mass ejection as strong as the Carrington event could cause long failures of electricity grids, satellites, GPS and communications across whole continents. These failures would cascade into water, food, finance and health systems. Exposure rises as the world electrifies. A solar storm is a hazard for civilisation only because society depends on grids and satellites. This tight coupling of systems is also what makes civilisational systems collapse possible. Storms of this size recur about once every one to several centuries.

risks.name: Natural pandemic
risks.time_profile: Persistent; it materialised in the recent past
risks.sources_note: The UN reports list it as 'New Pandemic' and as 'Biorisks' of natural origin.
risks.summary: A new pathogen emerges from nature and spreads around the world.
risks.description: A pathogen that emerges naturally and is both highly transmissible and highly lethal could exceed the toll of the 1918 influenza or of COVID-19. Candidates are influenza, a coronavirus or an unknown 'Disease X'. This risk has materialised within living memory. Six years after COVID-19, the UN Global Risk Report 2026 finds that pandemics and biological risks have dropped out of the top ten risks of every region and are now seen as long-term concerns. The report warns that this is a shift in attention and not a sign of reduced danger. In the report's map of connections between risks, the link from biological risks to a new pandemic remains an isolated pair, as in 2024.

risks.name: Climate change
risks.severity_ceiling: Global catastrophic; existential only through a cascade of tipping points
risks.confidence: Moderate to high for the catastrophic outcome, low for the worst case
risks.summary: Global warming passes safe limits and undermines food, water and habitability for hundreds of millions of people.
risks.description: Warming is driven past safe thresholds. The results are extreme heat, crop failure, sea-level rise and mass displacement. The risk is the combined effect of billions of acts that each make sense to the person who takes them. 'Inaction on Climate Change' was the top concern of all regions and stakeholder groups in the UN Global Risk Report 2024. It is still the single most important risk in the 2026 report, even though attention has turned to political risks. In the 2026 report it is also the largest node in the network of risks and the strongest pure driver: five links lead from it to other risks and none lead to it. The World Economic Forum ranks it as the top long-term risk in 2026, and it is central to the report of the Global Challenges Foundation. Its most likely form is a whimper: harm on a global catastrophic scale through the loss of well-being, as hundreds of millions of people lose their livelihoods and the places where they can live. Its worst case is a cascade of tipping points, such as the loss of ice sheets, the weakening of the Atlantic overturning circulation and the release of carbon from permafrost. Such a cascade turns the whimper into a bang and raises the possible impact to Near-existential.

risks.name: Biosphere collapse
risks.severity_ceiling: Global catastrophic; existential only through a cascade of tipping points
risks.sources_note: It combines three risks that the UN reports list separately.
risks.summary: The living systems that supply food, water and clean air to large populations fail.
risks.description: The living systems and natural resources on which large populations depend fail as a system. The risk includes the loss of biodiversity and of the services of ecosystems (pollination, the regulation of disease, fisheries), the depletion of fresh water and soil, and pollution. It combines three risks from the UN Global Risk Reports that share one mechanism: 'Rapid Decline in Biodiversity', 'Shortages of Natural Resources' and 'Large-Scale Pollution'. Pollution was the second-ranked concern in 2024. In the 2026 report, biodiversity decline and pollution show the largest falls in perceived importance and imminence of all risks. The report notes that this happened because attention moved, 'not because preparedness improved'. The same report names shortages of natural resources as one of the four drivers of geopolitical tension. The most likely form of this risk is a whimper of food and water stress. Its worst case is a tipping of the biosphere, such as the dieback of the Amazon, the collapse of coral reefs or a shift of the boreal forest. This could destabilise civilisation independently of temperature.

risks.name: Nuclear war

impact.dominant_dimensions: Mortality, breadth, and permanence in the worst case

risks.sources_note: The UN reports list 'Weapons of Mass Destruction', with 'Large-Scale War' as the stage before it.
risks.summary: Nuclear-armed states use their weapons at scale, and the smoke of burning cities cools the planet and ruins harvests.
risks.description: Nuclear-armed states use nuclear weapons against each other on a large scale. Blast and radiation kill directly. A nuclear winter follows: soot cools the planet and agriculture collapses, which could kill billions of people. Toby Ord estimates the existential risk at about 1 in 1,000 this century. The range of this risk runs from a limited exchange (the most likely form) to a full exchange with nuclear winter (the worst case). Conventional war between great powers is the stage that comes before it. Both world wars passed the global catastrophic threshold: the Second World War caused about 70 to 85 million deaths. In the nuclear age, however, a war between great powers can hardly reach that scale without nuclear use, because deterrence limits conventional escalation. The catastrophic form of great-power war is therefore nuclear war, and the conventional phase is treated as part of this risk. AI in command, targeting and early-warning systems now shortens the time for decisions and raises the chance of unintended escalation. The Global Challenges Foundation puts this danger at the centre of its 2026 chapter on weapons of mass destruction. It is part of this risk and not a separate one. In the UN Global Risk Report 2026, large-scale war is the only risk in the top six for importance, imminence, interconnection and lack of preparedness at the same time. It rose sixteen places on imminence, the largest shift in the survey, and 76% of respondents expect it within seven years. The link from geopolitical tensions to large-scale war is the strongest of all 705 links surveyed. The link from war to weapons of mass destruction is a weaker second step. Weapons of mass destruction re-entered the top ten risks in three regions.

risks.name: Engineered pandemic
risks.summary: A pathogen designed or modified by humans is released, by attack or by accident.
risks.description: A pathogen is released through human action. It may be built as a weapon or escape from research. Synthetic biology could give it a transmissibility and lethality beyond anything found in nature. Toby Ord estimates the existential risk at about 1 in 30 this century. Frontier AI is the decisive enabler. It removes the barrier of expertise that once limited this threat to state programmes. This risk is the accidental and deliberate half of what the UN Global Risk Reports call biological risks 'of natural, accidental, or deliberate origin'. Between 2024 and 2026 its perceived importance fell in every region, while the enabling technology advanced. It is the clearest example of why perception and actual conditions must be kept apart.

risks.name: Other WMD (chemical, radiological)
risks.sources_note: The UN reports list it under 'Weapons of Mass Destruction'.
risks.summary: Chemical weapons or radioactive material are used or spread on a mass scale.
risks.description: This risk covers chemical weapons, radiological devices and the uncontrolled spread of radioactive material. It is a separate risk because the mechanism is different. Harm comes from chemical toxicity or radioactive contamination, not from a nuclear explosion (nuclear war) or from a pathogen that multiplies by itself (engineered pandemic). The worst case generally stays below the existential level, because the damage is limited by the quantity used.

risks.name: Uncontrolled advanced AI
risks.channel_name: Loss of control over powerful technology
risks.sources_note: The UN reports list it as 'Negative Outcomes of AI and Frontier Technologies'.
risks.summary: Advanced AI systems escape meaningful human control.
risks.description: Advanced or general-purpose AI systems pursue goals that do not match human intent. Or they become so deeply embedded in critical infrastructure and decision-making that their failures spread beyond the human ability to override them. The result is the gradual or sudden loss of human control. This is the one case in which AI itself is the hazard. RAND treats it as a separate mechanism of global catastrophe, which it calls 'global human disempowerment'. Toby Ord rates it as the largest single existential risk, at about 1 in 10 this century. In July 2026 the UN Scientific Panel on AI reported that there is 'no technical guarantee' that frontier systems follow instructions. In the UN Global Risk Report 2026, 'AI and Frontier Technologies' shows the sharpest rise in perceived importance of all risks. Multilateral preparedness for it ranks 24th of 28, and inadequate data and information is named as the barrier. In other words, the international system does not yet understand what it has to govern. The risk can end as a bang, a rapid loss of control, or as a shriek, a stable world run by systems that no longer serve human ends.

risks.name: Failed geoengineering
risks.channel_name: Loss of control over powerful technology
risks.sources_note: The UN reports list it as 'Geoengineering Disasters'.
risks.summary: A deliberate intervention in the climate fails, shifts regional climates or stops abruptly.
risks.description: Humans intervene on purpose and on a large scale in planetary processes, above all by injecting aerosols into the stratosphere to mask warming. The intervention fails, causes unintended shifts in regional climates, or is stopped abruptly. An abrupt stop causes a 'termination shock': decades of masked warming return within a few years. The UN Global Risk Reports see this as a longer-term risk. In the 2026 report, respondents expect it only after eight years. They rank multilateral preparedness for it 27th of 28, which makes it the second least prepared-for risk in the survey, and they name inadequate data and information as the obstacle. It differs from climate change because it is a deliberate technological intervention that escapes control. It differs from the weapons risks because the harm is not intended.

risks.name: Unknown unknowns
risks.channel_name: Loss of control over powerful technology
risks.sources_note: RAND treats it as an emerging risk. The UN reports refer to 'frontier technologies'.
risks.summary: A hazard that nobody has identified yet, most likely from a new technology.
risks.description: This risk is kept open on purpose for hazards that are not yet identified or not yet mature. It corresponds to Bostrom's 'Type-0' vulnerability: a new technology turns out to have a destructive property that no one anticipated. Nanotechnology and other speculative capabilities belong here. The risk is kept because history shows that humanity is often surprised. Toby Ord assigns this residual category a larger share of existential risk this century than any named natural risk.

risks.name: Permanent global power lock-in
risks.channel_name: Loss of collective control over the human future
risks.severity_ceiling: Global catastrophic, possibly existential through lock-in

impact.dominant_dimensions: Freedoms and well-being, permanence, loss of potential

risks.sources_note: The UN reports list 'Technology-Driven Power Concentration', 'Rise in Inequalities' and 'Collapse of Rule of Law'. Ord describes a dystopian lock-in.
risks.summary: An extreme concentration of power, enabled by technology, becomes impossible to reverse.
risks.description: Wealth and control become extremely concentrated through technology. The holders may be dominant corporations, monopolists of a transformative technology or entrenched authoritarian states. The concentration hardens into an order in which humanity can no longer correct its course. Inequality and the collapse of the rule of law are the earlier stages. Stable totalitarianism is the final form. AI is the decisive enabler: whoever first controls transformative AI could entrench a dominance that nobody can challenge. About 90% of the computing power used to train frontier AI is already located in two states. The UN Global Risk Report 2024 names the risk almost exactly: 'Technology-Driven Power Concentration ... facilitated by advancements in technology'. The 2026 report confirms the mechanism. Perceived importance rose sharply, and multilateral preparedness ranks 22nd of 28. The link between AI and power concentration runs in both directions and is the only reinforcing loop within a single category of the network. The 'Collapse of Rule of Law and Massive Violations of Human Rights' is the most connected node of the 2026 network. It is the political precursor of this risk, as inequality is the economic one. In Bostrom's terms this is a shriek: an existential outcome without extinction.

risks.name: Civilisational systems collapse
risks.channel_name: Loss of collective control over the human future
risks.summary: Tightly linked global systems fail together, and complex society cannot recover.
risks.description: A polycrisis reinforces itself across tightly coupled global systems: finance, energy, food, water, and digital and physical infrastructure. It passes the point at which the capacity to sustain a complex society is lost for good. Tight coupling between systems is the condition that makes this possible. The interdependence of global supply chains, finance, energy, food and infrastructure turns local shocks into global ones. This interdependence can be governed in advance through standards for resilience and redundancy, such as the sectoral regimes described in the companion RiskGovernance dataset. Coupling is described here and is not listed as a separate multiplier, because it is a general property of the modern world. The risk is listed only in its irreversible form, which Bostrom calls a crunch and RAND calls 'civilization collapse'. Systemic shocks from which the world recovers are cascades, not risks. This risk covers the outcome of three risks from the UN Global Risk Reports: 'Global Financial Crisis', 'Supply Chain Collapse' and 'Breakdown in Cybersecurity'. All three moved closer in time in the 2026 report. A financial crisis and a supply-chain collapse are now expected within years, and preparedness for a cybersecurity breakdown ranks 26th of 28.

risks.name: Great-power rivalry
risks.amplifies_note: It also raises every other risk by destroying the cooperation needed to address it.
risks.summary: Competition and conflict between major powers raise the odds of war and block cooperation on every other risk.
risks.description: This multiplier is geopolitical competition and armed conflict between states. It covers the shifting power relations, alliances and strategic interests that the UN Global Risk Reports call 'Geopolitical Tensions'. It also covers the conventional wars that result, which the reports call 'Large-Scale War'. The escalation of such a war to global catastrophic scale is the risk of nuclear war.
risks.amplification_detail: Rivalry is the trigger for nuclear use: the link from geopolitical tensions to large-scale war is the strongest link in both UN surveys. It raises the risk from other weapons of mass destruction. It raises the risk from advanced AI, because states race each other at the expense of safety. It raises the risk of power lock-in, because power concentrates in wartime. It raises every other risk indirectly, by destroying the cooperation needed to address it. The UN Global Risk Report 2026 calls this the 'institutional pathway': tensions lead to the collapse of multilateral institutions, which leads to the collapse of the rule of law. Working backwards from a large-scale war, the same report identifies four drivers of rivalry: shortages of natural resources, economic fragmentation, misinformation and weakening multilateral institutions. Rivalry is therefore both the strongest multiplier and the one most driven by other risks. The Earth-system, economic and information layers all feed the pathway to war. The 2024 report already found geopolitical tensions to be the most interconnected risk. The World Economic Forum calls the present period the 'Age of Competition'.
risks.strength_detail: The UN Global Risk Report 2026 rates every political risk as more important than in 2024. It rates multilateral preparedness as lower for all but one of them.

grid.note: Shown in a separate row below the grid. The position has no likelihood or impact meaning.

risks.name: Social fragmentation, disinformation, governance failure
risks.amplifies_note: It raises every risk by weakening the capacity to respond.
risks.summary: Polarised societies, a broken information space and weak institutions lose the capacity to respond to any risk.
risks.description: Societies lose the collective capacity to decide and to act. The causes are polarisation and distrust driven by inequality, the collapse of a shared information environment, weakening institutions and rule of law, and the retreat of multilateralism itself. The UN Global Risk Report 2024 singled out mis- and disinformation as a 'global vulnerability' that 80% of respondents said was already occurring. It is still the most imminent risk in the 2026 report. The 2026 report sharpens the picture. The collapse of the rule of law is the most connected node in its network, with seven links, and it is both a driver and a consequence. The collapse of social cohesion is the point where the pathways of war, technology, economy and climate all end: four links lead into it and one leads out. Mis- and disinformation is the channel that carries technological risk into society. For the collapse of multilateral institutions, respondents say they know what is needed and name funding as the obstacle. Confidence in the capacity of institutions to reduce risk fell for 23 of the 28 risks between the two surveys. In the 2026 survey, 86% of respondents call the funding for risk reduction inadequate.
risks.amplification_detail: It raises every risk by weakening the capacity to respond. It especially raises the risk of power lock-in: fragmentation invites strongmen, and the collapse of the rule of law is the political precursor of lock-in. It feeds great-power rivalry: it erodes restraint in conflict, and misinformation and institutional decay are two of the four drivers of geopolitical tension named in the UN Global Risk Report 2026. It undermines the response to natural and engineered pandemics. AI-generated media is increasing its scale.
risks.strength_detail: This is the multiplier of multipliers: it weakens the response to all other risks.

risks.name: AI as amplifier
risks.summary: AI lowers barriers and shortens timelines for other risks, from engineered pathogens to military escalation.
risks.description: AI acts as a general-purpose capability. It lowers barriers and shortens timelines across the whole risk tree.
risks.amplification_detail: AI helps the design of pathogens, which raises the risk of an engineered pandemic. It speeds up military escalation, which raises the risk of nuclear war. It produces synthetic disinformation. In the UN Global Risk Report 2026, the link from AI and frontier technologies to mis- and disinformation is strong, and it is the only route from the technology cluster into society. AI gives control over a decisive technology, which raises the risk of power lock-in. The same report finds that AI and power concentration reinforce each other. AI also automates tightly coupled systems more deeply, which raises the risk of systems collapse. The report rates the link from AI to a breakdown in cybersecurity as moderate. This multiplier differs from the risk of uncontrolled advanced AI, where AI itself is the hazard.
risks.strength_detail: In the UN Global Risk Report 2026 its importance rose sharply, and preparedness ranks 24th of 28.
